title: Move match-engine off the 2021 EC2 worker AMIs onto EKS
subtitle: Two-phase cutover. Cost, on-call load, and deploy time. Do not wrap the AMI in a DaemonSet.
author: Aman Kumar
audience: Priya Nair (EM), Diego Alvarez (SRE). Copy Kavya Menon and Jordan Hale (platform).
owners: Aman Kumar (memo and Phase 1 charts), Priya Nair (go/no-go), Diego Alvarez (cluster clh-prod-eks-01)
summary: Recommend moving Clearhaven match-engine off the 18-host EC2 worker fleet (AMI ami-0c8f4e2a baked March 2021, ssh snowflakes since) onto the existing EKS cluster clh-prod-eks-01 in us-east-1. Do it in two phases: ingest-api and break-svc first (four weeks), match-engine second (six weeks after Phase 1 is boring). This memo is for Priya Nair and Diego Alvarez. It covers cost ($47.3k/mo today vs $31.8k/mo modeled), on-call (AMI drift caused three incidents in 2023, 14.6 hours combined Sev-2), and deploy time (4.2 hours median bake-and-roll vs 18 min helm). Reject wrapping the 2021 AMI in a DaemonSet. That idea showed up in CH-PLT-4418 and it dies here with numbers.
form_description: Internal recommendation memo from Software Engineer II Aman Kumar to the Clearhaven engineering manager and SRE lead, arguing for a two-phase EKS migration of match-engine compute and rejecting an AMI-in-DaemonSet shortcut.
revision_history: Draft after CH-PLT-4418 review with Diego. Cost table from AWS Cost Explorer, account 184920337661.
Added the three 2023 AMI-drift incidents and the DaemonSet rejection. Priya asked for a two-phase plan, not a single cut.
Phase dates, node group sizes, and open questions. Jordan Hale reviewed the terraform bits.
Approved for Priya/Diego. Status Approved after standup. No scope change.

blocks.text: Recommendation

blocks.label: Decision asked
blocks.text: Yes: move match-engine compute to EKS in two phases. Phase 1 (ingest-api, break-svc) start November 13, 2023. Phase 2 (match-engine Deployment, 12 replicas, c6i.2xlarge node group me-ng-01) start January 8, 2024 if Phase 1 has gone 21 days without a compute-related Sev-2. Do not lift the 2021 AMI into a DaemonSet. Priya owns go/no-go. Diego owns the cluster and the node group. Aman owns the Helm charts and the cutover runbook CLH-RB-2023-031 (draft).

This is the compute memo Priya asked for after the September 8 incident (CLH-INC-2023-157). Match-engine still runs on 18 EC2 instances in asg-me-workers-prod, launch template lt-08b21c4e, AMI ami-0c8f4e2a. That AMI was baked March 11, 2021 by whoever owned packer/match-engine at the time. The packer repo has had 11 commits since, none of them applied to prod. Operators ssh in, apt-get a library, leave a comment in the Slack thread, and we pretend the next instance will look the same. It does not.

Diego already runs clh-prod-eks-01 for the recon API, the Kafka Connect cluster (connect-clh-prod, 6 pods), and the Grafana agent. Node groups recon-ng-01 and connect-ng-01 have been boring since July. The question is whether match-engine, which pins 6.2 GiB RSS at peak and talks Unix sockets to a local redis-sidecar we never should have put on the box, belongs there too. Short answer: yes, after we stop treating the worker as a pet. The redis-sidecar moves to ElastiCache clh-matchkey-prod (ticket CH-PLT-4502, Kavya is already in that design). The Unix socket goes away. That is a Phase 2 prerequisite, not a reason to stay on EC2.
Why this is on your desk now

Three Sev-2s in 2023 trace to AMI drift. I sat with Diego and pulled the pager timestamps from PagerDuty service match-engine-prod. Combined customer-visible impact was 14.6 hours. Combined engineer time, including the Friday night where Jordan and I rebuilt openssl on me-worker-07b by hand, was 41.2 hours. Helen Cho's ops queue absorbed 2,184 extra exception rows on September 8 because match-engine was 11.4 minutes late into the 16:00 ET settlement window. Marcus Bell had to tell the RailClear TAM the file would miss their 16:15 cutoff. We made it at 16:18. They accepted it. That is not a process we get to repeat.

Deploy time is the other reason. A match-engine release today is: bump the version in the bake Jenkins job job/clh/match-engine-ami, wait 52-67 minutes for packer, copy AMI to the launch template, start an instance refresh on asg-me-workers-prod, watch 18 hosts cycle, ssh to the first three because the userdata script races chrony, then run /opt/clearhaven/bin/me-smoke.sh. Median wall clock from merge to smoke green: 4.2 hours. P95: 6.8 hours. We did this 19 times in 2023 through October 31. Helm on the same cluster, for ingest-api which we already containerized in staging, is 18 minutes merge to ready, 11 minutes if the image is cached. I timed both last Thursday.

Cost is third, not first. I would still write this memo if EKS were more expensive, because the incident math is worse than the invoice. It happens EKS is cheaper once we drop the 18 always-on c5.2xlarge boxes and stop paying for 40% idle CPU at 02:00 ET. Modeled number is $31.8k/mo versus $47.3k/mo. Details below. Jordan Hale pulled Cost Explorer. I did not round his numbers.
Current fleet

asg-me-workers-prod sits in vpc-0a17c4e8821 (clh-prod), subnets subnet-0b2e91a (use1-az1) and subnet-07c44d2 (use1-az2). We never got az3 because the 2021 bake assumed two AZs and nobody wanted to re-bake. Security group sg-0e91c3aa allows 22/tcp from the old bastion bastion-prod-01 (i-0aa12f44, also a snowflake) and 9092/tcp egress to the MSK cluster clh-msk-prod. Match-engine listens on 8443. The ALB me-prod-alb still points at instance targets. Health check is /healthz every 15s, 3 failures, which is why a stuck JVM can sit in the ASG for 47 seconds before traffic drains. We have known that since the March incident.

blocks.text: I am not going to print all 18 rows here. Priya has the sheet. The point is there is no two-host pair you can call identical. userdata.sh in the launch template still writes /etc/clearhaven/me.conf from a 2021 template that references kafka-legacy.prod.clearhaven.internal, which is a CNAME Diego left behind when MSK cut over in January. Match-engine ignores that file if /etc/clearhaven/me.conf.local exists, and me.conf.local exists on 14 of 18 hosts because someone scp'd it during the MSK cut. The other four read the stale CNAME, fail over to the bootstrap list in the JVM flags, and work anyway. Until they do not.
The three 2023 AMI-drift incidents

I want these in the memo because 'the AMIs are fine, we just need better change control' was the counter-argument in CH-PLT-4418. Change control on a fleet you ssh into is a wish. Here is what actually happened.

blocks.caption: Sev-2s in 2023 where the root cause was host drift, not application code. Times ET.
rows: Kafka TLS handshake failures after a broker cert rotation
openssl 1.1.1f on 6 hosts, 1.1.1k on 12. Bake was 1.1.1k. The 6 never got the March 2022 hotfix.

RailClear file 11 min late. Marcus on the phone. 2,184 extra exception rows. Helen still references this in standup.

blocks.text: CLH-INC-2023-041 is the one that still bothers me. We rotated the MSK broker certs on a Thursday because the previous cert expired Friday. Six workers could not complete the handshake. Those six were the ones that had never been recycled since 2021. The launch template said the AMI had openssl 1.1.1k. osquery said otherwise. Diego's post-incident note was 'stop sshing into prod.' We did not stop. We added a runbook step that says check openssl version before a cert rotation. That is treating the symptom.

CLH-INC-2023-089 is on me as much as anyone. Kavya had a core dump. Jordan and I installed gdb and a newer glibc on me-worker-07b because the AMI image did not have debug symbols and we did not want to wait 4.2 hours for a bake. The process came back, looked fine, then died 16 hours later in a matching hot path that called a glibc symbol we had just moved. The binary and the host no longer agreed. That is the snowflake failure mode in one paragraph.

CLH-INC-2023-157 is the one Helen will quote if we try to delay this. Four hosts had ntpd, fourteen had chrony, the security group change on September 7 blocked UDP 123 from the ntpd boxes to time.google.com (that was a Diego ticket, CH-OPS-2281, correct change, wrong assumption that every worker used chrony). Clock skew hit 11.4 minutes. Match-engine's event time vs wall clock check started dropping batches as 'future.' We caught it because the 16:00 ET settlement file was thin, 61.2% of expected legs. Helen called Marcus, Marcus called Priya, Priya called me. I sshed in, installed chrony, and we still missed RailClear's cutoff by 3 minutes. They took the file. Ops spent the weekend in the exception queue.
Cost

Numbers from AWS Cost Explorer, linked account 184920337661, service filter EC2-Instances plus EKS plus ElastiCache plus data transfer, August and September 2023 averaged. Jordan Hale exported the CSV on October 18. I am not using list prices.

blocks.text: Caveats Priya will ask about. The $15.5k/mo is not cash until Phase 2 is done and we terminate the ASG. Phase 1 overlap will cost more for 4-6 weeks because ingest-api already runs on 4x c5.xlarge (asg-ingest-prod, $3,640/mo) and will dual-run on EKS. I budgeted $4.1k extra for November and $2.7k for December. If Phase 2 slips to February the overlap on match-engine is ugly: we would pay both the ASG and me-ng-01. Do not slip. The mixed-instances policy is Diego's. He will not put match-engine on more than 30% spot after the April MSK spot experiment stole a broker. I agree.

The ElastiCache line is real cost we currently hide on the worker. Local redis on the box is why we cannot run more than one match-engine process per host and why a pod cannot reschedule without losing the matchkey cache. Kavya's ElastiCache write-up is in CH-PLT-4502; for this recommendation we treat clh-matchkey-prod as a Phase 2 gate, not a nice-to-have. If ElastiCache is late, Phase 2 waits. We do not put redis in the pod and call it a migration.
On-call load

PagerDuty service match-engine-prod, January 1 through October 31, 2023. I exported incidents with tag compute or host or ami. Application bugs are out of scope for this memo; Rahul can fight those separately.

blocks.text: Thirty-two compute-tagged pages in ten months. Three Sev-2s. The recon API on EKS, same PagerDuty, same ten months: four compute-tagged pages, zero Sev-2, all node-group autoscaler delays under 8 minutes. Sample size is not huge. Direction is not subtle. Diego's on-call doc for clh-prod-eks-01 is three pages and the common fix is 'look at the deployment, not the box.' Match-engine's host runbook is 19 pages and still missed chrony.

I also timed how long a new on-call takes to become useful. Sneha Iyer shadowed me in August. For ingest-api staging on EKS she found the pod, the logs, and the last helm revision in 12 minutes. For match-engine prod she spent 40 minutes figuring out which of 18 hosts had the bad openssl, because the Datadog host map still used the 2021 naming regex and me-worker-07b had been renamed in inventory but not in the agent config. That 40 minutes is the snowflake tax. It does not show up in Cost Explorer.
Deploy time

I sat through two production match-engine deploys (October 12 and October 26) with a stopwatch, and one ingest-api staging helm deploy (October 26, same afternoon). Chris Patel was on the October 12 call because the bake touched a JNI flag he cares about. Numbers below are wall clock, merge of the version bump to smoke green.

blocks.caption: Deploy wall clock. Match-engine is today's path. ingest-api staging is the path Phase 1 copies.

helm upgrade --wait, 8.2 min for 6 pods, maxUnavailable 1

previous launch template version, another instance refresh, 2.1-3.4 hours
helm rollback, 4-9 min on this cluster (timed on recon-api last month)

blocks.text: Rahul asked whether we can just parallelize the AMI bake. We can shave maybe 15 minutes. We cannot shave the instance refresh unless we double the ASG and run 36 hosts during deploy, which is a $1,580 experiment per release I will not sign. Helm already does surge. That is the whole point of a Deployment.
Rejected: lift the AMI into a DaemonSet

blocks.label: Rejected alternative
blocks.text: CH-PLT-4418 comment 12 (Jordan Hale, October 6): run the existing AMI as the node image, put match-engine in a DaemonSet so every node still looks like me-worker-N, keep ssh via SSM, keep local redis. Diego marked it 'worth a look.' It is not. This section is why it died.

The pitch is tempting if you squint. We already have EKS. Bottlerocket and AL2023 node AMIs make Diego nervous for a JVM that still loads a JNI library built on Ubuntu 20.04. If we keep ami-0c8f4e2a as the node AMI, the JNI library keeps working, local redis keeps working, and we tell leadership we 'moved to Kubernetes' in Q4. I wrote a spike. It ran in the staging account for nine days. Here is what broke.

DaemonSets are per-node, not per-workload. Match-engine needs 12 replicas at peak and 6 at night, not 'one per node of a 12-node group.' If we size the node group to 12, we pay for 12 at 02:00 ET, which is the cost problem we already have. If we size to 6 and DaemonSet that, we cannot burst to 12 without adding nodes, which is slower than a Deployment replica change (node join on this cluster is 4.6-7.1 minutes; pod start is 18-40s). HPA on a DaemonSet is a fiction. I will not file a ticket to invent one.

The AMI is still a snowflake, just now it is the node. Packer still takes 52-67 minutes. Node AMI roll on EKS is worse than an ASG instance refresh because kubelet drain, pod reschedule, and the DaemonSet maxUnavailable dance stack. I timed a node AMI bump on recon-ng-01 in staging in September (Diego's AL2023 test): 2.8 hours for 8 nodes, and recon pods rescheduled cleanly because they are stateless. Match-engine with local redis on the node would drain by losing cache. We would be doing the September incident on purpose every deploy.

ssh via SSM to a Kubernetes node that also runs kubelet, the Datadog agent, and a JVM is how you get the June incident again. Someone will gdb a process. glibc will move. The node will disagree with the container, except now the container is not even a container, it is a hostPath mount of /opt/clearhaven from the AMI. I opened that mount in the spike. It works. It is also the opposite of why we are doing this.

JNI is a real constraint. The library libmejni.so is built on Ubuntu 20.04, glibc 2.31, and it dlopen's from /opt/clearhaven/lib. Phase 2 ships a container FROM ubuntu:20.04 with that library in the image, not on the node. Kavya already does this in the staging Dockerfile repo/match-engine/Dockerfile.staging. The spike proved the JNI load works in a container on an AL2023 node. We do not need the 2021 AMI under kubelet to keep JNI. We need the library in the image. That work is a week, not a reason to DaemonSet a fossil.

Jordan agreed in the October 27 review. The comment on CH-PLT-4418 now says 'DaemonSet path closed, see CLH-MEM-2023-027.' If someone reopens it, send them this section. Do not spike it again. Nine days was enough.
Two phases

Priya asked for a plan that does not put match-engine, ingest-api, and break-svc on a new scheduler in the same weekend. Agreed. Phase 1 is the two services that are already containerized and already run in staging on clh-staging-eks-01. Phase 2 is match-engine plus ElastiCache plus killing asg-me-workers-prod.

blocks.caption: Phase plan. Dates assume Priya says yes this week and we do not freeze for the Thanksgiving file.
rows: ingest-api and break-svc images in ECR, Helm charts in repo/clh-charts, staging soak 47 days
No open Sev-2 on staging EKS for those two services
ingest-api prod to clh-prod-eks-01, namespace clh-ingest, 8 replicas, node group ingest-ng-01 (6x m6i.xlarge)
p99 ingest 12-40s stays inside the current 40 min SLA (we are already at ~9 min post-Kafka; do not regress past 12 min p99)
break-svc prod, namespace clh-break, 4 replicas, same ingest-ng-01 (fits)
Helen Cho exception queue depth < 400 at 18:00 ET for 3 days

ElastiCache clh-matchkey-prod, dual-write from match-engine EC2
cache hit rate >= 94.2% vs local redis baseline 96.1% (we accept 2 points)

smoke + 48h shadow vs EC2 (see commands below)
asg-me-workers-prod desired=0, 14 day wait, then terminate and delete launch template

blocks.text: Phase 1 does not wait on ElastiCache. ingest-api and break-svc do not use the local redis. That is why they go first. If Phase 1 blows up we still have match-engine on EC2 and we still settle. If we did match-engine first and the cluster hiccuped, Helen's Monday morning is wrecked. I want the cluster to have eaten two more production services before we put the matching hot path on it.

Thanksgiving week is Nov 20-24. 1b sits on Nov 20-22, which is tight. If Priya wants a freeze from Nov 20, we slide 1b to Dec 4-6 and accept that Phase 2 slides a week. I would rather slide than cut break-svc the Monday before a short settlement week. Rahul, please say this out loud in planning so nobody 'just ships it Friday.'
What Phase 1 looks like for a working engineer

This section is the part you execute, not the part you present. Cluster is clh-prod-eks-01, region us-east-1, account 184920337661. kubecontext prod-clh. Charts in github.com/northstar-eng/clh-charts, paths ingest-api/ and break-svc/. Values files values-prod.yaml. Image repo 184920337661.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/clh/ingest-api.

blocks.caption: Phase 1a cutover sketch. Full command list will live in CLH-RB-2023-031. Do not paste this into prod without Diego on the call.
blocks.text:
# context
aws eks update-kubeconfig --name clh-prod-eks-01 --region us-east-1 --profile clh-prod
kubectl config use-context arn:aws:eks:us-east-1:184920337661:cluster/clh-prod-eks-01

# node group (already applied in terraform, CH-PLT-4502)
# module.eks_clh_prod.aws_eks_node_group.ingest_ng_01
# instance_types = ["m6i.xlarge"]  desired=6  min=4  max=10

kubectl get ns clh-ingest || kubectl create ns clh-ingest
kubectl -n clh-ingest apply -f ./rbac/ingest-api-prod.yaml

helm upgrade --install ingest-api ./ingest-api \
  --namespace clh-ingest \
  --values ./ingest-api/values-prod.yaml \
  --set image.tag=1.18.4 \
  --wait --timeout 12m

kubectl -n clh-ingest rollout status deploy/ingest-api --timeout=10m
kubectl -n clh-ingest get pods -o wide
# expect 8 Running, spread across at least 3 nodes, 2 AZs minimum

# flip ALB target group ingest-prod-tg from instance to IP, register pod IPs
# terraform apply -target=module.alb_ingest.aws_lb_target_group_attachment
# keep asg-ingest-prod desired=4 for 48h

# smoke
curl -sS --max-time 5 https://ingest.prod.clearhaven.internal/healthz
# expect {"status":"ok","broker":"clh-msk-prod","lag_ms":<400}

# abort
helm rollback ingest-api 1 -n clh-ingest --wait
# then terraform apply the instance target group again

Health checks. ingest-api /healthz must see MSK (bootstrap b-1.clh-msk-prod.c7.kafka.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:9092) and Postgres clh-recon-prod.cluster-c8a1.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com. If the pod comes up and /healthz is ok but lag_ms is 12,000, you did not fail the deploy, you failed the consumer. Do not helm rollback for lag. Check the consumer group ingest-api-prod-cg on topic clh.settlement.inbound. That is a different runbook (CLH-RB-2023-012).

break-svc is the same chart pattern, namespace clh-break, image break-svc:2.4.9, 4 replicas, shares ingest-ng-01. It talks to Postgres table break.exception_queue and to match-engine over gRPC on 8443. Until Phase 2, that gRPC still hits the EC2 NLB me-prod-nlb. Do not point break-svc at a Kubernetes Service for match-engine in Phase 1. There isn't one yet. I will put a ClusterIP in Phase 2b and flip break-svc then. Mixing that flip into 1b is how we get a two-cause outage.
Phase 2 shadow and cut

Match-engine on EKS runs as Deployment match-engine, namespace clh-match, 12 replicas, resources requests 3 CPU / 8Gi, limits 4 CPU / 10Gi (today's c5.2xlarge is 8 vCPU / 16 GiB; we were wasting it; 4 CPU is enough at 12 replicas, I measured 2.7 CPU p95 on the hot host during October month-end). Pod anti-affinity preferred, not required, because required anti-affinity plus 12 pods plus 12 nodes is how you fail a rollout when one node is cordoned.

Shadow for 48 hours means both EC2 and EKS consume the same Kafka topic clh.settlement.inbound, EKS uses a distinct consumer group match-engine-eks-shadow, and we diff match results into s3://clh-prod-artifacts/me-shadow/YYYY-MM-DD/. Chris Patel has a Spark job for that diff (he used it on the Kafka ingestion cut). Accept if the shadow disagrees on <= 0.04% of legs, which is the same bar we used in May. If it disagrees more, stop, do not flip the ALB.

items: Confirm ElastiCache clh-matchkey-prod replication group available, failover test done by Kavya, CH-PLT-4502 closed.
helm upgrade --install match-engine ./match-engine -n clh-match --values values-prod.yaml --set consumerGroup=match-engine-eks-shadow --set replicas=12 --wait.
Run Chris's diff job for 48 hours covering one weekday close (16:00 ET) and one overnight batch.
Priya go/no-go. If yes, helm upgrade --set consumerGroup=match-engine-prod and pause the EC2 consumers (systemctl stop me.service on two hosts first, then the rest).
Flip ALB me-prod-alb target group to IP targets of the pods. Keep EC2 processes stopped but instances up for 14 days.
Smoke: me-smoke Job, Helen spot-checks 20 breaks, Marcus confirms RailClear file size within 0.8% of T-1.

blocks.text: Failure modes
JNI load fails on AL2023 nodes

Symptom: CrashLoopBackOff, log line 'libmejni.so: ELF class mismatch' or 'glibc GLIBC_2.32 not found' (the second one means someone built the .so on a newer box). Check: kubectl -n clh-match logs and ldd inside a debug copy of the image. Fix: rebuild libmejni.so in the Ubuntu 20.04 builder we already have, do not upgrade the node AMI to 'make it work.' Rollback: stay on EC2. This is a Phase 2 blocker, not a Phase 1 problem.
HPA fights the matching hot path

If we scale from 12 to 16 during a burst, Kafka rebalances. We already know the staging rebalance in October took 38s and stalled matching. Cap maxReplicas at 14 until we have cooperative sticky assignor on the EKS consumer. Diego, please keep cluster-autoscaler from deleting a node under a match-engine pod during 15:30-16:30 ET. Annotation cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict=false on the pod template.
Local redis leftover in the image

Someone will copy the staging Dockerfile and leave redis-server as a sidecar 'just for Phase 2a.' That sidecar will split-brain with ElastiCache. Image scan should fail if redis-server is in PATH. Sneha, add that to the QA checklist. If it ships anyway, the symptom is matchkey hit rate oscillating 40-95% as pods disagree. Kill the sidecar. Do not 'tune' it.
AZ3 Kafka partition skew

MSK is 3 AZ. Workers today are 2 AZ. Moving to 3 AZ node groups will change cross-AZ bytes (cost table already has +$1,460). It can also change consume latency by 4-12ms. That is fine. If someone sees p99 ingest jump 2 minutes, it is not AZ3, it is the consumer. Check lag first.
ssh muscle memory

On-call will try to SSM to the node and restart the JVM. Nodes will not have me.service. The runbook has to say kubectl -n clh-match rollout restart deploy/match-engine and mean it. I will put that sentence at the top of CLH-RB-2023-031. If we leave SSM open with sudo, we will recreate me-worker-07b inside a node. Diego: lock SSM to session-only, no sudo, on me-ng-01. That is a Phase 2c gate.
What we are not doing

items: Not moving MSK. clh-msk-prod stays. Kafka ingestion redesign is a different memo (CLH-MEM-2023-004, already done).
Not moving Postgres. clh-recon-prod stays on RDS. Partitioning is CLH-TDD-2023-011.
Not introducing a service mesh. No sidecar for mTLS beyond what the JVM already does to MSK.
Not Bottlerocket for me-ng-01 in Phase 2. AL2023. JNI tests passed there. Bottlerocket can be a 2024 follow-up if Diego wants it for recon-ng first.
Not a Friday cut. Not a month-end cut. Not the Monday after a long weekend.

blocks.caption: Open questions. Owners named. Dates are when the answer is due, not when the work finishes.
rows: Confirm mixed-instances 70/30 on-demand/spot for me-ng-01, or 100% on-demand for the first 60 days?
I recommend 100% on-demand until soak ends. $3,180 is not worth a spot kill during 16:00 ET.
Helen: exception queue SLO during Phase 1b. Is depth < 400 at 18:00 ET the right exit, or do you want age < 25 min?
Marcus can proxy if Helen is in month-end.
JNI rebuild in the Ubuntu 20.04 builder: who signs the artifact?
Today the .so is copied off me-worker-02a. That has to die before Phase 2.
Do we keep bastion-prod-01 after Phase 2c, or is SSM-on-nodes enough?
Bastion is another snowflake. I want it gone. Security may disagree.
Rahul: is there a customer communication for the Jan 15-19 cut, or is this internal-only?
No protocol change. File times should not move. Marcus thinks TAM note is still polite.
cluster-autoscaler window 15:30-16:30 ET: scale-down disabled how? Annotation only, or a schedule?
Annotation on the pod is the minimum. A schedule is better.

blocks.text: Ask of Priya and Diego

Priya: approve the two-phase plan, including the November 13 Phase 1a start, or tell me to slide 1b past Thanksgiving. Do not approve a DaemonSet. Do not approve a single weekend where all three services move. I need a yes or a dated no by November 8 so Kavya can lock the ElastiCache order (cache.r6g.xlarge is not always sitting in us-east-1 the week you want it).

Diego: own clh-prod-eks-01 node groups ingest-ng-01 and me-ng-01 in terraform, mixed-instances decision, SSM lockdown on me-ng-01, and the ALB IP target group change. I will not apply terraform that touches the cluster without you on the PR. Also: please put the chrony incident in your SRE review so this does not read as an application team dumping hosts on you. It is a shared mess. I am trying to make it a shared Deployment instead.

If you want the short version for leadership: we spend $47.3k/mo on 18 pets that caused three Sev-2s this year and take 4.2 hours to deploy. EKS on the cluster we already have is $31.8k/mo modeled, 18 minute deploys, and we stop sshing into openssl. Two phases. JNI in the image. Redis off the box. No DaemonSet. I will write the runbook once Priya says yes.
